title: Leyden papyrus X
venue: Wikipedia (tertiary encyclopedia; cites the primary literature listed on the page)
ask_addressed: What textual and material evidence shows alchemy / early chemistry in Greco-Roman Egypt (Alexandria, Panopolis): Leiden papyrus X, Stockholm papyrus, Pseudo-Democritus Physika kai Mystika, Zosimus of Panopolis, Mary the Jewess (Maria Prophetissa) and her apparatus, Cleopatra the Alchemist? Dates, languages, and what they actually describe (practical dye/metal recipes versus theory).
quote: The presentation is exclusively practical, and does not include the usual alchemical or philosophical elements.
summary: Greek codex of c. end of 3rd century CE with 111 recipes on metals, imitation gold/silver, stones, purple dye and inks; the article says it is purely practical, with no alchemical theory.
limits: Page gives dates as c. 250 to end of 3rd century; does not itself test the transmutation question. Tertiary, editable encyclopedia article: use it to locate the primary editions and scholarship it cites (Halleux 1981, Lagercrantz 1913, Caley, Berthelot, Lindsay 1970), not as final authority. Authorship and year not stated.

quote: there are two sciences and two wisdoms, that of the Egyptians and that of the Hebrews
summary: Zosimos, of Panopolis (Akhmim), flourished c. 300 CE and wrote in Greek (parts survive in Syriac/Arabic); his works mix apparatus descriptions with visionary and Hermetic allegory, and he comments on an older Democritus text.
limits: The page's claim that his imagery parallels pharaonic motifs (Amduat) is an interpretation, not evidence of pharaonic alchemy.
